title: Annual health checks and health action plans
blurb: Explain who is eligible for a learning disability annual health check, what it covers and how the health action plan turns it into action.
question: Lucy, 33, has a mild learning disability and lives alone with a few hours of support a week. She has never been invited for an annual health check. Her support worker asks the community nurse why. What is the most likely reason, and what should happen?

teach.h: A yearly check designed to close the health gap
teach.body: Anyone aged 14 or over who is on their GP practice's learning disability register can have a free annual health check once a year. A doctor or nurse checks physical and mental health, looks for conditions that are more common in people with a learning disability, reviews medicines and agrees actions. In plain English: it is a planned, adjusted check-up that catches problems early, because people with a learning disability often do not report symptoms or get the same care.

items.label: About a quarter on a GP register

teach.caption: Being on the register also opens the door to flu vaccine priority and recorded reasonable adjustments.

head: Area
Examples
rows: Urine or blood tests if needed
Are they still right? Side effects?

steps.label: Adjusted invitation
steps.sub: Easy read, longer slot, quiet time

steps.label: Annual health check
steps.sub: With someone who knows the person

teach.h: Scenario: Lucy has never been invited
teach.body: Lucy, 33, lives alone with a little support and has never had an annual health check. The likely reason is that she is not on her GP's learning disability register: only about a quarter of people with a learning disability are. With Lucy's agreement, the nurse asks the practice to add her. If the practice declines, the community learning disability team can help. Once registered, her invitation and appointment are adjusted to suit her.

NICE NG11 says GPs should offer an annual physical health check to all people with a learning disability, using a standardised template, with a family member or carer who knows the person well. It should look at links between behaviour that challenges and physical health, and review medicines and their side effects. NG54 adds mental health, and for adults with Down's syndrome asks about changes in behaviour, loss of skills or needing more prompting, which may point to dementia.

teach.caption: NG96 lists age-related conditions to monitor, including hearing, sight, thyroid problems, osteoporosis and dementia.

items: Invite in easy read with pictures, and phone the person or their supporter.
Book a longer appointment at a quieter time, with a carer if the person wants.
Use the person's communication methods and explain each step before doing it.
Write adjustments in the health action plan so they are used next time.
If someone does not attend, find out the barrier instead of just sending another letter.

teach.text: The check starts at 14, not 18, which links it to transition planning. And it is offered to people on the GP learning disability register: someone who is not on the register will not be invited, however clear their needs are.

items: Free annual check from age 14 for people on the GP learning disability register.
Only about a quarter of people with a learning disability are on a register.
Covers measurements, tests, epilepsy, constipation, dysphagia, sight, hearing, medicines, vaccines, carers.
Actions go into a health action plan; adjustments are written down too.
NG11: with someone who knows the person; NG54: mental health and Down syndrome dementia questions.

summary: You can now explain who can have an annual health check, why the GP register matters, what the check covers and how the health action plan carries actions forward. You can also add the NICE extras for behaviour, medicines, mental health and Down syndrome.

A.q: Mia, 14, has a moderate learning disability and is on her GP practice's learning disability register. Her mother asks the school nurse whether Mia can have a learning disability annual health check yet. What is the correct answer?
options: No, the checks start when she turns 16
No, the checks start at 18 when she transfers
Yes, a free check is offered each year from age 14
Yes, after a referral from a paediatrician
A.why: Anyone aged 14 or over on the GP learning disability register can have a free annual health check once a year.

whyNot.1: The check starts before transfer to adult services, at 14.
whyNot.3: No paediatric referral is needed; being on the register is what matters.

A.q: Jordan, 29, has a learning disability. At his annual health check the practice nurse finds raised blood pressure and that he has not seen a dentist for years. Where should the agreed actions be recorded?
options: In a health action plan agreed with Jordan
In his hospital passport for future admissions
In a letter to his support provider
On the Reasonable Adjustment Digital Flag
A.why: Outcomes and agreed actions from the annual health check are written in the health action plan.

whyNot.1: The hospital passport supports admissions; it is not where check actions are planned.
whyNot.2: A letter to the provider is not an agreed plan with Jordan himself.
whyNot.3: The flag records reasonable adjustments, not health actions.

A.q: Ahmed, 41, has a severe learning disability and limited speech. His GP practice is booking his annual health check. Following NICE NG11, who should ideally attend with him?
options: A hospital learning disability liaison nurse
A family member or carer who knows him well
A social worker from the local authority
An independent mental capacity advocate
A.why: NG11 1.2.1: the annual health check should be carried out with a family member or carer who knows the person.

whyNot.0: NG11 asks for someone who knows the person; a hospital liaison nurse mainly supports hospital care and does not know Ahmed's usual self as his family or carer does.
whyNot.2: NG11 includes a social care practitioner only if they know the person; a local authority social worker is not described as knowing Ahmed well.
whyNot.3: An IMCA is instructed for specific decisions when no one is appropriate to consult.

B.q: Lucy, 33, has a mild learning disability and has never been invited for an annual health check. Her nurse finds she is not on the GP learning disability register. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Book her a standard NHS health check instead
Wait for the practice to identify her at age 40
Ask a hospital consultant to refer her for checks
With Lucy's agreement, ask the practice to add her
B.why: The register is the gateway to annual checks. With her agreement she can ask the practice to add her; if declined, the community learning disability team can help.

whyNot.0: A standard check is not adjusted for her and does not replace the learning disability check.
whyNot.1: Waiting leaves her without the checks she is entitled to now.
whyNot.2: No hospital referral is needed to join the GP register.

B.q: Simone, 37, has Down syndrome and attends her annual health check with her support worker. She has no new symptoms. Which test should be part of her yearly check?
options: A thyroid function blood test
A routine brain scan
A resting electrocardiogram
A bone density scan
B.why: Hypothyroidism is common in Down syndrome and risk rises with age, so thyroid testing is done every year for life.

whyNot.1: Routine brain scans are not part of the annual check.
whyNot.2: An ECG is not a routine yearly test without a clinical reason.
whyNot.3: Bone density scans are not a routine yearly test.

B.q: Kieran, 26, has a learning disability and takes an antipsychotic prescribed for behaviour that challenges. His nurse is helping the GP plan his annual health check. Under NICE NG11, what should it include?
options: A test of his IQ to update his records
A plan to increase the dose if behaviour worsens
His medicines and side effects, and behaviour-health links
A capacity assessment for every medicine he takes
B.why: NG11 1.2.1: the check should review medicines and side effects and consider links between behaviour that challenges and physical health.

whyNot.0: IQ testing is not part of the annual check.
whyNot.1: Increasing medication is not a check item and runs against STOMP principles.
whyNot.3: Capacity is decision-specific and presumed; it is not assessed for every medicine at the check.

C.q: Jamal, 31, is autistic with a learning disability. He has not attended his annual health check for two years; a standard letter was sent each time. What is the most appropriate next step for the practice?
options: Remove him from the register as he does not attend
Send the same letter again by recorded delivery
Wait until he next contacts the practice himself
Find out the barriers with Jamal and his supporters
C.why: Non-attendance often reflects barriers such as inaccessible letters, waiting rooms or anxiety. The practice should explore them and plan adjustments.

whyNot.0: Removal would block his access to checks and adjustments.
whyNot.1: Repeating an inaccessible letter does not remove the barrier.
whyNot.2: Waiting leaves him without checks; the duty to adjust is anticipatory.

C.q: Paula, 46, has Down syndrome. At her annual health check her sister says that over recent months Paula needs more prompting to dress and has lost interest in her hobbies. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Reassure her sister this is normal ageing for Paula
Arrange thyroid tests and a dementia assessment
Recheck at next year's annual health check
Refer Paula to a day centre for more activities
C.why: NG54 1.5.4: changes in behaviour, loss of skills or needing more prompting may suggest the need for dementia assessment. Thyroid problems, which can mimic dementia, must also be checked.

whyNot.0: This is diagnostic overshadowing; the change needs assessment.
whyNot.2: Waiting a year delays assessment of a significant change.
whyNot.3: Activities may help, but the cause of the change must be assessed first.

C.q: A practice nurse is designing an annual health check template for people with a learning disability. Which conditions does NHS guidance highlight to check because they are more common?
options: Epilepsy, constipation and swallowing problems
Asthma, eczema and hay fever
Migraine, gout and kidney stones
Psoriasis, glaucoma and varicose veins
C.why: NHS guidance highlights conditions more common in people with a learning disability, including epilepsy, constipation and dysphagia, plus eyesight and hearing.

whyNot.1: Long-term conditions like asthma are reviewed if present, but these are not the conditions highlighted as more common.
whyNot.2: These are not the conditions highlighted for this group.
whyNot.3: These are not the conditions highlighted for this group.

reteach.title: Register, check, plan
reteach.question: What three things must be in place for an annual health check to make a difference?

blocks.body: First the person must be on the GP learning disability register, from age 14. Then the check must be adjusted and done with someone who knows them. Finally the results must go into a health action plan that is followed up. Break any link and the benefit is lost.

blocks.text: Non-attendance is a signal to adjust, not a reason to remove someone from the register.

explain.body: Aged 14 or over and on the GP learning disability register. Only about a quarter of people with a learning disability are registered, so getting people on the register is a nursing priority.

items.label: people with LD on a register

test.q: What must be true for a person to be invited for a learning disability annual health check?
options: They have a diagnosis confirmed by a psychiatrist
They are aged 14+ and on the GP LD register
They live in a registered care home or supported living
They have a social worker or care coordinator
test.why: Eligibility is age 14 or over and being on the GP learning disability register.

whyNot.0: A psychiatric diagnosis is not the entry requirement.
whyNot.2: People living independently or with family are eligible too.
whyNot.3: Having a social worker is not required.

explain.body: Weight, heart rate, blood pressure; tests if needed; epilepsy, constipation, dysphagia, eyesight and hearing; medicines review; vaccinations; long-term conditions; wellbeing and carer support.

test.q: Which of these is part of a learning disability annual health check?
options: Assessing eligibility for disability benefits
Checking the person's housing tenancy
Updating the person's employment record
Reviewing whether medicines are still right
test.why: The check includes a review of whether medicines are still appropriate.

whyNot.0: Benefits assessments are separate from the health check.
whyNot.1: Housing is not part of the health check.
whyNot.2: Employment records are not part of the health check.

explain.body: Results and agreed actions, plus the reasonable adjustments the person needs, are written down in the health action plan so they are followed up and used next time.

test.q: A nurse wants to make sure the longer appointment and picture explanations that helped Ravi at his check are used next time. Where should they be recorded?
options: In his health action plan or health profile
In a note on the practice noticeboard
In his next invitation letter
In the practice's complaints log
test.why: NHS guidance says reasonable adjustments should be written down in the health profile or health action plan.

whyNot.1: A noticeboard is not a confidential record.
whyNot.2: An invitation letter does not record needs for future care.
whyNot.3: The complaints log is for complaints, not care planning.

explain.body: NG11: with someone who knows the person; behaviour and physical health links; medicines and side effects. NG54: mental health; Down syndrome changes suggesting dementia. Down syndrome: yearly thyroid test.

test.q: At an annual check for an adult with Down's syndrome, which question does NICE NG54 recommend asking?
options: Whether they want to stop all their medicines
Whether they have lost skills or need more prompting
Whether their family wants a care home place
Whether they have any new hobbies this year
test.why: NG54 1.5.4: ask about changes in behaviour, loss of skills (including self-care) or needing more prompting, which may suggest the need for a dementia assessment.

whyNot.0: Stopping all medicines is not a recommended check question.
whyNot.2: Placement is not part of this NICE recommendation.
whyNot.3: Hobbies may come up, but the recommended question is about loss of skills and prompting.
